extracted.intended_audience: interactive fiction authors, designers, and interested players thinking about choice and narrative design
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of how 'choice' functions in interactive fiction, contrasting calculation-based decisions with conflict-driven choices, and surveying design patterns (parser IF vs choice-based IF, expressive choices, granularity, etc.). Useful for authors designing choice mechanics and narrative branching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation vs Choice (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations = 'decisions based solely on reason with a clear correct answer'; Choice = 'overcoming internal conflict'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to classify player decisions. Examples: avoiding a scorpion is a calculation; fighting one more mob for level-up vs avoiding loss is a choice because it pits competing desires. The taxonomy helps judge whether a decision is about reasoning/optimization or about resolving internal tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of meaningful dilemma/conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A true dilemma exists only if choice A and choice B are of roughly equal importance; choices should resolve internal conflict to qualify as 'choice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether options force trade-offs that create tension. Robert McKee / Choice Poetics referenced: 'a dilemma exists only if choice A and choice B are of equal importance.' Examples: morally fraught options (e.g., throw someone to the wolves vs turn them in) that affect the protagonist's future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence magnitude / branching significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between cosmetic/fluff choices (lead to small text differences) and consequential choices (affect story, endings, or game state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games that offer few large branches make it easier to track 100% completion; games with many small choices increase immersion but are harder to exhaustively map. Prefer significant branching when aiming for divergent narrative outcomes; choose 'fluff' choices when aiming for frequent player expression or micro-variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced trade-offs / scheduling/resource dilemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Design situations where players must divide scarce resources (time, attention, funds) between mutually exclusive important objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Jolly Good: Cakes and Ale' where multiple life-important events are scheduled simultaneously; such forced trade-offs generate real choices and dramatic tension. Use scheduling conflicts to create difficult, meaningful decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roleplay vs mechanical optimization tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the mechanically optimal action is plain; players may choose non-optimal options for roleplay or narrative reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Choice of Rebels — stealing is mechanically better but players may avoid it for roleplay. When evaluating choices, account for whether the design allows meaningful roleplay divergence from pure calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard mode / permanence of choices (undo/no-undo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the game allows undo/reloads influences how choices are perceived; 'hard mode' or no-undo makes decisions weightier and can make calculation-heavy games frustrating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of Games examples: games with no undo increase the emotional cost of choices. Decide whether to allow reversibility based on intended tension and player expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive decisions / identity-defining choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices that let players express identity (gender, romance, persona) or make cosmetic selections that may nonetheless influence story and character relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These can be purely cosmetic or have significant downstream effects; treat expressive options as a separate category from calculation/conflict decisions. They can meaningfully affect engagement without being about optimization or dilemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity / 'particles' (microscopic vs macroscopic interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser IF often offers a 'vista of particles' — many small interactive elements and verbs — whereas choice-based games operate at a coarser granularity (few discrete options).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use granularity to decide interaction design: parser games support exploration and many small interactions (EXAMINE MAILBOX) that are not high-stakes choices; choice games favor clearly defined options that must be tracked in branching structures. Consider how granularity affects player experience (exploration vs decision tension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration as distinct decision category
rubrics_metrics.description: Some player actions (exploration, inspection, experimental inputs) are neither calculations nor choices by the earlier definitions; they serve discovery rather than conflict-resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games like Galatea highlight exploratory interactions that are about discovery and interpretation. Evaluate IF for whether it supports meaningful exploration separate from branching choice mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching-for-endings vs choice-based gameplay distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate games where choices only pick an ending (gameplay is calculation/puzzle-driven) versus games where the gameplay itself is driven by choice-based decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Slouching Towards Bedlam (puzzles with several resolutions) vs Kerkerkruip or Floatpoint (gameplay is choice-driven). When designing, decide whether choices should permeate mechanics or primarily determine endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of choices: 'fluff' vs sparse significant choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Designers must choose between many small, frequent choices (fluff) and a few rarer, high-impact choices; player preferences vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual novel community divides on this: some prefer few significant branches (easier to 100%); others prefer many small choices for immersion. Consider target audience and completion/achievement expectations when setting choice frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player agency and emergent narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Choices should enable players to create emergent narratives for themselves; player actions and reactions can generate satisfying, personalized stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for opportunities where player decisions yield coherent emergent arcs (even from limited mechanics). Example: single-room game where player's attempts and responses to an NPC generate emergent narrative feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of choices / link usage
rubrics_metrics.description: How choices are presented (links, menus, text) matters; 'links are the most important new punctuation mark...' — interface affects pacing and perception of agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study small essays (On Links: Exercises in Style) and Emily Short's pieces on interfaces to choose how to signpost and present choices. Interface decisions change how players read and interact with choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding cruelty and frustrating calculations in parser IF
rubrics_metrics.description: Parser IF design often avoids 'cruelty' — mechanics that punish exploratory calculation in ways that are unfair or excessively frustrating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parser games typically discourage high-cost trial-and-error calculations; when creating puzzles or branching, ensure players aren't unfairly penalized for curiosity or reasonable experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of future outcomes (foreshadowing/hints)
rubrics_metrics.description: When options are genuinely equiprobable, reason can't decide; designers can use hints/foreshadowing to reduce pure randomness or to deliberately keep outcomes ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want choices to be meaningful rather than random, provide foreshadowing or signaling. Conversely, if equal-likelihood dilemmas are desired, accept that some players will choose randomly and design for that.
